client: I've been really struggling since my dog passed away last month. It's like all the little things that used to make me happy just... don't anymore. I go through my day feeling kind of hollow, and honestly I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything.
therapist: What you're describing — that hollowness, the loss of the small joys — makes complete sense after losing a companion who was woven into the fabric of your everyday life. I also notice you mentioned some doubt about whether talking will even help, and I want to gently honor that skepticism rather than brush past it — it's okay to feel uncertain about this process. What would it mean to you if talking *did* help, even just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess if talking helped even a little, it would mean I'm not just stuck like this forever, which honestly is one of my bigger fears right now. But it's hard to imagine because I've tried talking to friends about it and they kind of just say things like "he had a good life" or "you'll feel better soon," and it doesn't really touch what I'm actually feeling. So I think part of me is worried this will be more of the same.
therapist: The fear of being stuck forever is such a painful thing to carry, and it makes sense that those well-meaning but surface-level responses from friends have left you feeling unseen rather than comforted. What you're describing — that unnamed thing that "he had a good life" just doesn't touch — I'm curious, if you could put words to what *is* actually there, what do you think it might be?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: I think what's actually there is this really specific kind of loneliness, like he was the one constant in my day who was just... always happy to see me, no judgment, no expectations. And now I come home and the apartment is so quiet, and there's nobody waiting, and it makes me realize how much of my sense of not being alone was tied up in him. It's embarrassing to even say out loud because I feel like I should have more people in my life who fill that role, and the fact that I don't makes me feel kind of pathetic.
therapist: What you just described isn't pathetic at all — that bond was real, and the role he played in your daily sense of connection and belonging was genuinely significant, regardless of whether it came from a person or an animal. I also notice you spoke about all of this very quickly, like the words needed to get out before something stopped them — and I wonder if part of you has been holding that "embarrassing" label over this grief, which might be making it even heavier to carry. What would it feel like to let go of the idea that you *should* feel differently than you do?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, the idea of letting go of that "should" feels kind of relieving to think about, but also almost impossible in practice. Like, I know intellectually that the grief is valid, but there's this other voice that keeps comparing me to people who have lost actual family members or gone through bigger things, and it makes me feel like I don't have the right to be this wrecked over a dog. I'm not sure how you just decide to stop feeling like you're being self-indulgent.
therapist: That comparing voice is so common, but it's worth noticing that grief isn't a competition where only the "biggest" losses earn the right to hurt — your nervous system doesn't measure loss in those terms, even if that critical voice tries to. The shift from "letting go of the should" feeling relieving *in theory* to impossible *in practice* is actually really important — it tells me the intellectual understanding is already there, and what we'd be working on is helping the rest of you catch up to what you already know. What do you think that comparing voice is trying to protect you from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That's a question I wasn't expecting, and I have to sit with it for a second. I think maybe the voice is trying to protect me from... feeling like I'm falling apart over something I "shouldn't" be falling apart over, like if I minimize it first, then nobody else can make me feel worse about it. But saying that out loud makes me realize I've basically been doing the criticizing to myself before anyone else gets the chance, which is kind of a sad way to operate.
therapist: What you just uncovered is genuinely significant — that pattern of beating yourself to the punch, criticizing yourself before anyone else can, is a form of self-protection that makes a lot of sense given how unsafe it must feel to be vulnerable about this. And there's something quietly brave in the way you said that, like part of you recognized the sadness of it even as the words were coming out. What do you think it would feel like to be on your own side for once, the way your dog always was?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: That question actually made my eyes sting a little, which I wasn't expecting. I think being on my own side would feel like... relief, but also really unfamiliar, like I genuinely don't know how to do that without it feeling self-indulgent again, which I guess just proves your point. He never once made me feel like I was too much or not enough, and I don't know how to give that to myself when I can barely even accept that I deserve to grieve him.
therapist: The fact that this brought tears tells me something in you *knows* that you deserve that gentleness, even if the knowing and the feeling aren't quite connected yet. What you had with him — that unconditional acceptance — wasn't something you stumbled into by accident; you also showed up for him every day, which means you already know how to offer that kind of care. I wonder if the work ahead isn't about learning something entirely new, but about slowly turning toward yourself with even a fraction of what you so naturally gave to him.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That reframe is actually kind of beautiful, and part of me wants to hold onto it, but I also immediately think "okay but how do I actually do that in practice when I come home to that quiet apartment and just feel the absence of him everywhere." Like the concept makes sense here in this room, but I'm not sure it survives contact with real life, especially in those specific moments when the grief just hits out of nowhere. I guess I'm asking whether there's something more concrete I can actually do, or is it more about just... sitting with it?
therapist: That's such an honest and important question, and the fact that you're already anticipating the gap between insight and real life shows real self-awareness. There *are* concrete things we can work with — like creating a small, intentional ritual for those moments when you walk through the door, something that acknowledges his absence rather than fighting it, which can help your nervous system feel less ambushed by the grief. But I'm also curious — when you imagine coming home tonight, what's the very first moment that tends to hit hardest?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It's the sound of my keys in the lock, because for years that sound meant he would start moving around and making noise on the other side of the door, and now there's just nothing. I stand there for a second before I even open it, like I'm bracing myself, and then I walk into the silence and it just kind of confirms the loss all over again every single time. I'm open to the idea of a ritual but I honestly don't know what that would even look like, and I'm a little worried it might feel forced or hollow, like I'm just going through motions.
therapist: The keys in the lock becoming a trigger makes so much sense — that sound was the beginning of being *met*, and now it's the beginning of absence, so your whole body has learned to brace before you even open the door. A ritual doesn't have to be elaborate or feel meaningful right away — it could be as simple as pausing at that moment with your keys and saying his name out loud, just once, as a way of acknowledging him rather than bracing against the silence. It might feel a little awkward at first, but the goal isn't to feel better immediately — it's to give that moment *something* instead of just the void.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Saying his name out loud actually feels both right and terrifying at the same time, like it might make it more real instead of less painful, which I know is probably the point but it's still scary. I think part of me has been trying to get through those moments by going numb and moving fast, so deliberately slowing down and acknowledging him feels like the opposite of what my instincts are telling me to do. I think I could try it, but I'm genuinely not sure I won't just start crying in my hallway every night, and I don't know if that's okay or if it means it's not working.
therapist: Crying in your hallway every night isn't a sign that it's not working — it's actually a sign that you're finally letting the grief move through you instead of outrunning it, and that's exactly what healing looks like even when it feels awful. The instinct to go numb and move fast makes complete sense as a way to survive, but grief tends to wait patiently for us, so slowing down isn't creating the pain — it's just finally letting you meet what's already there. You don't have to get it perfect; even trying it once, even if you cry, would be a kind thing to do for yourself.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: "Grief tends to wait patiently for us" is something I think I'm going to be turning over in my head for a while, because it actually makes the numbness feel less like coping and more like just... delaying something inevitable. I think I can try saying his name once, just once, and see what happens, even though every part of me is already preparing to feel ridiculous or fall apart. I guess what I'm realizing is that falling apart in my hallway alone is maybe not that different from what I'm already doing inside, just more honest about it.
therapist: What you just said — that falling apart honestly might not be so different from what you're already doing inside — is one of the most courageous things you've said today, and I want you to really hear that. I notice you arrived at something that sounds like a quiet breakthrough, but there's something in your voice that feels like it's carrying more weight than the words alone, like part of you is still bracing even as another part is opening up. Be gentle with yourself as you try this — you're not just experimenting with a ritual, you're practicing the very thing your dog always gave you freely, and that's no small thing.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
